abstract: Choanoflagellates, the closest known living relatives of animals, provide a powerful comparative system for investigating the evolution of extracellular morphology and cell behaviour on the animal stem lineage. Although all choanoflagellates share a conserved cellular architecture including a flagellum and collar of microvilli, they display a wide diversity of extracellular structures and behaviours throughout the life cycle. Their extracellular features, historically used for species identification, have long been suspected to reflect a mixture of evolutionary inheritance and ecological plasticity. Yet, the majority of choanoflagellate diversity remains undescribed, and the extent to which their extracellular traits map onto their phylogeny has remained unclear, impeding comparative reconstructions of the evolutionary history of extracellular structures with the earliest animals. Here, we integrate super-resolution fluorescence imaging, electron microscopy and transcriptomic analysis to characterize the extracellular structures and behaviours across both currently described lineages of choanoflagellates (Craspedida and Acanthoecida), by studying pairs of closely related species in conjunction with novel isolates representing previously unexplored clades. Our results reveal strong conservation of extracellular morphology between close relatives, whereas deeper evolutionary distances uncover unexpected innovations, such as sheath-like layers, bipartite thecae, crawling stages and atypical inverted division patterns. Furthermore, the inclusion of early-branching taxa sister to the loricates supports the hypothesis that the silicified extracellular lorica is a derived trait rather than an ancestral feature. Together, our findings suggest that the last choanoflagellate common ancestor possessed an organic non-silicified extracellular covering composed of one or more layers and that it was capable of both swimming and crawling behaviours, refining the cellular context from which animals evolved.
hook: Animals' closest relatives descend from an ancestor with a soft coat that could swim and crawl.
summary: Choanoflagellates are the nearest living relatives of animals. Imaging and transcriptome data from described species and new isolates suggest their last common ancestor had an unsilicified, layered outer covering, and the glassy lorica evolved later. The ancestor is inferred from living species, so the reconstruction rests on sampled lineages.
title: The extracellular morphology and behaviour of the last common ancestor of animals and choanoflagellates
